newsitem.title: USA: US YIELD CURVE- Bond makes bid to push below 7 pct.
newsitem.headline: US YIELD CURVE- Bond makes bid to push below 7 pct.

text.p: What was thought to be nearly impossible just a few weeks ago is now close to becoming a reality: the U.S. Treasury 30-year bond breaking below the psychologically important 7.0 percent threshold.
After all, in late March the Federal Reserve had begun what many perceived to be the first in a mini-string of rate hikes, pushing both short and long term yields higher.
The 30-year bond just last week had tested the 7.20 percent level, and analysts had figured it was only a matter of time before the bond would breach 7.25 percent on its way to 7.30 and above.

But a combination of fundamental (weak data) and technical (massive short covering) factors this week brought Treasuries off their lows, pushing long term yields to levels not seen since March 26 -- a day after the Fed tightened credit. On Thursday morning, the bond yield fell as low as 7.05 percent.
"It shows how oversold the market was the last couple days," said Matthew Alexy, chief Treasury market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp.
Alexy noted that the 7.06 percent support level had been in place for a few weeks, and should it fall below, the next technical level is around 6.96 percent.
Analysts noted that to get to 7 percent, the June bond contract has to only rise to 108-1/2 -- about a 1/2-point above where it currently stands.

The latest rally was triggered by a surprisingly weak consumer price report on Tuesday, which forced many short positions to cover. And even after a strong industrial production report on Wednesday pushed the market down, another wave of short-covering rescued the market.
The buying continued following what was described as a mixed but mostly bond-friendly set of economic data on Thursday morning.
Jobless claims rose by 8,000 to 332,000 in the week ended April 12, and most of the components of the Philadelphia Fed's April business outlook survey were down.
"If we get a few more reports like those I wouldn't rule out a move below 7 percent," said Douglas Schindewolf, money market economist at Smith Barney Inc.

"The market backed up quite a bit and is now consolidating," he said. "Plus or minus 10 basis points of 7 percent is where we will hang out until we get a signal one way or another on continued economic strength or an economy beginning to moderate."

The downdraft in bond yields comes at a time when market sentiment remains bearish and in a market that still expects the Fed to raise rates another 1/4-point at its May or July policy setting meeting.
"It's a pretty technical type of market," Alexy said. "The question for the long end is where value is offered ... and what the next likely trade is."

With little in the way of key economic data until the first quarter employment cost index is released on April 29, chances are considered decent the bond will test 7 percent, especially if data continue to come in on the weak side.

"Sentiment is so negative now that any piece of information that would begin to sway people's minds about the fundamentals could create buyside activity," said John Spinello, government securities strategist at Merrill Lynch & Co.
